analysis.one_liner: Requires clear labels on genetically engineered foods and bans calling them 'natural'.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: 53 House members from both parties backed it, but the Energy and Commerce Committee took no action on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended federal food law to bar the sale of any genetically engineered food, or food with genetically engineered ingredients, unless its label clearly said so. It also would have banned labeling such foods as 'natural' or similar words, and set small exemptions for restaurant food, medical food, foods under 0.9% genetically engineered content, and foods using genetically engineered vaccines or processing aids. It offered protections so farmers and food handlers would not be penalized for unintentional trace contamination, and treated certified organic food as non-genetically engineered by definition.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who want to know how their food is produced. The bill's stated purpose was to give shoppers knowledge of whether their food was genetically engineered, for health, economic, environmental, religious, and ethical reasons, and to prevent confusing or misleading 'natural' claims on engineered foods [S3]. Shoppers in the more than 60 countries that already require such labeling — including the EU, Japan, China, and Brazil — had this information; US shoppers would have gained the same disclosure [S3]. Organic farmers and independent certifiers also benefit, because the bill treats certified organic food as non-GE and relies on independent testing organizations, giving them a defined legal status and a compliance role [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires that any genetically engineered food, or food containing genetically engineered ingredients, carry a clear disclosure on its ingredients label before it can be sold [S2] [S3].
Bans labeling or advertising genetically engineered foods as 'natural', 'naturally made', 'naturally grown', or 'all natural', to prevent consumer confusion and deception [S2] [S3].

Protects small players: restaurants, medical foods, packaged foods under 0.9% genetically engineered content, and foods using GE vaccines or processing aids are exempt, and farmers are not penalized for unintentional contamination not due to their negligence [S2] [S3].

Treats certified organic food as non-genetically engineered and lets independent organizations certify non-GE status through internationally consistent testing, giving organic producers a clear compliance path [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that sell genetically engineered foods and foods containing engineered ingredients — seed developers, ingredient processors, and packaged food makers — bear the cost of testing, segregation, recordkeeping, and label changes. Some of that cost can be passed to shoppers through prices. Companies using 'natural' marketing on engineered foods would have to drop those claims [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs for tracking, segregating, testing, and relabeling ingredients fall on food companies and would partly show up in consumer prices; the bill allows a 0.9% tolerance precisely because keeping products perfectly free of engineered material is costly and difficult [S2] [S3].

A good-faith objection supporters would have to answer: the bill's own findings note FDA already requires labeling of more than 3,000 ingredients, additives, and processes, but regulators have generally treated engineered foods as safe, so opponents argued the label implies a hazard where the science sees none — the bill responds that the fact is of 'material importance to consumers' regardless [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is information: shoppers who avoid engineered foods for any reason — health, religious, ethical, or environmental — get a consistent national standard instead of a patchwork of state laws and 'natural' marketing claims. The main cost is compliance spending by food and seed companies, some fraction of which reaches grocery prices. The bill is written to blunt the sharpest objections — exemptions for restaurants and trace amounts, safe-harbor guaranties for food handlers, and negligence-based protection for farmers facing accidental cross-contamination — so the tradeoff is modest compliance cost in exchange for disclosure the bill notes more than 60 countries already require [S2] [S3].

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee: the House referred it to Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced, the panel sent it to its Health Subcommittee, and neither took up the bill before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter DeFazio introduced the Genetically Engineered Food Right-to-Know Act on February 12, 2015, with 24 original cosponsors listed on the bill [S3].

Fifty-three members cosponsored the bill — 52 Democrats and 1 Republican — but it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee on February 13, 2015, and no further action was ever recorded [S1] [S4] [S5].
The bill's action history ends at the subcommittee referral; it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote in the 114th Congress [S5].

The following year, Congress instead enacted a separate, weaker federal labeling standard that lets companies satisfy disclosure through QR codes and website links rather than on-package text — the approach this bill, requiring clear on-label disclosure, did not take (widely reported; not in the provided sources).

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Food and biotech companies that sell genetically engineered products are better off: no federal labeling mandate ever reached a vote, and the disclosure standard later enacted was more flexible for industry. Shoppers did not get the on-package disclosure this bill promised.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, listed among the original sponsors in the bill text

against.role: Packaged food and beverage industry trade group

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic — 52 of the 53 cosponsors were Democrats, with a single Republican — and the bill died in a committee controlled by the Republican majority without a vote.

industries.note: A mandatory on-package GE label applies to foods made from their engineered crops and ingredients, which the bill's findings describe as affecting export value and sensitive markets. Their commercial interest in unlabeled products runs against shoppers' stated desire for disclosure [S3].

They would bear testing, segregation, recordkeeping, and relabeling costs, and would have to drop 'natural' claims on engineered products. The industry's push to avoid mandatory labeling conflicts with the disclosure the bill would guarantee shoppers [S2] [S3].

industries.industry: Organic food producers and independent certifiers
industries.note: Certified organic food is deemed non-GE by definition, and independent organizations gain a defined role certifying non-GE status through standardized testing. Their interest in verifiable labels matches what shoppers asked for [S2] [S3].
Retailers face new shelf-label and supplier-verification work, but they also sell the organic and labeled products shoppers would be better able to identify. Gains and losses roughly balance.
